## Statistical Approach
Our initial statistical assessments revealed that many features across nearly all data sources exhibited extreme right-skew. Because severe skew distorts linear regressions and distance-based machine learning models, we implemented several transformation strategies. First, any skewed features received a logarithmic transformation. For features containing zero values, NumPy's log1p function was used to prevent undefined log-zero errors; otherwise, the standard log function was used. For algorithms such as PCA, random forests, neural networks, and logistic regression, where some features retained enough skew after logarithmic transformation and standardization to degrade model performance, we initially scaled features using scikit-learn’s StandardScaler. To fix this, we adopted scikit-learn's QuantileTransformer. By mapping feature values to a uniform or normal distribution based on quantiles, this approach successfully mitigated the impact of extreme outliers and normalized our inputs for downstream modeling.

Our dataset exhibited severe class imbalance, as the vast majority of county-year observations contained zero data centers. Left unaddressed, this imbalance caused significant prediction bias and poor performance in our machine learning models. We leveraged built-in class weighting mechanisms (such as class_weight='balanced' in scikit-learn's LogisticRegression) to assign higher penalty weights to errors on the minority class during training. In cases where the balanced weight parameter didn’t improve the model or was unavailable, we applied SMOTE to generate synthetic instances within the feature space of the minority class, rebalancing the training distribution.
While initial evaluations included classical statistical frameworks like linear and logistic regression, these models yielded limited explanatory power and low statistical significance. Consequently, we adopted Difference-in-Differences (DiD) as our primary analytical framework. This shift was supported by prior literature in the field and the method's ability to isolate treatment effects and support stronger causal inferences regarding data center deployment.

We evaluated multiple treatment definitions within the DiD framework. We initially defined treatment as any county transitioning from zero data centers in a prior year to one or more in the subsequent year. Ultimately, we observed stronger statistical significance when defining treatment as a county transitioning from two data centers in a given year to three or more in the following year. This stronger statistical signal likely reflects two factors: first, a larger regional cluster of data centers produces a more pronounced economic impact that is easier to detect above baseline noise; second, this higher threshold minimizes potential sensitivity to the imputation methods applied to resolve missingness in the QCEW NAICS 518 dataset.

## Machine Learning Approach
During exploratory analysis, we used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to examine the underlying geometric structure of our dataset. Projecting the data onto the first two principal components revealed distinct structural patterns across county observations. When visualizing these projections, we observed clear spatial separation between counties with and without data centers. Crucially, this separation persisted even when training the PCA model on a feature set that explicitly excluded the data center count. Color-coding the projection by the log-transformed data center count (applied due to extreme right-skew from high-density outlier counties) reinforced this pattern. The underlying feature set cleanly separated counties based on data center presence, suggesting fundamental structural differences in local economic and demographic profiles.
To formalize these subgroupings and test whether different county types respond differently to data center deployment, we implemented k-means clustering. We evaluated various cluster counts using the silhouette score to quantify separation. Across iterations, k=2 consistently yielded the highest silhouette score. Passing the top principal components into the k-means algorithm rather than raw features further improved cluster separation and maximized the overall silhouette score.

Mapping cluster assignments spatially revealed geographic clusters even without spatial coordinates or centroid locations included in the input features. Comparing summary statistics across both groups confirmed that cluster assignment primarily aligned with population density and economic scale. Consequently, we interpreted Cluster 0 as predominantly rural counties and Cluster 1 as urban counties, aligning our empirical grouping with existing literature that stratifies local economic impacts along rural and urban lines.

We used k-means clustering because we suspected that distinct classes of counties would respond differently to an additional data center. Logically, some counties are much larger in terms of population and economic activity, meaning a new data center, even a large one, would have a minimal effect relative to the overall economy. By testing various cluster counts, we found that k=2 provided the best separation. 
While our k-means clustering model yielded two distinct groups, the approach introduced trade-offs compared to traditional binary classifications. The primary advantage of multi-feature k-means clustering is that it optimizes mathematical separation across the entire feature space, improving downstream model performance. However, this comes at the cost of interpretability. Because the model ingested a broad set of economic and demographic variables (excluding explicit geographic coordinates and data center counts), the resulting clusters reflected complex, multidimensional similarities beyond a simple rural versus urban split. Running PCA on the full feature set introduced potential data leakage risks relative to downstream targets. To resolve this and improve model transparency, we restricted a second pass of the PCA and k-means pipeline strictly to baseline structural predictors: total population and physical county area.

Mapping and evaluating summary statistics for this refined two-cluster split produced geographic and demographic distributions nearly identical to our initial run. This confirmed that population density and county scale drive the underlying structural separation while significantly boosting model interpretability and preventing feature leakage.

The VAE was designed to extend our Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework. While DiD provides a quasi-experimental comparison between treated and control counties, the VAE learns a continuous latent representation of each county's unique socio-economic trajectory. By identifying the specific vector within the VAE's latent space that corresponds to variations in data center count, we can perturb that direction while holding all other latent features constant. Reconstructing the output from this modified latent code creates a synthetic counterfactual effectively simulating a parallel universe where an identical county experiences data center deployment under otherwise identical baseline conditions.
We chose a Variational Autoencoder over a standard deterministic autoencoder specifically for its smooth, continuous, and regularized latent space. This continuous manifold ensures that moving along the "data center vector" in latent space traverses valid, meaningful states rather than unpopulated or unstable gaps.

One of the main challenges in training the Variational Autoencoder was defining an appropriate validation strategy. Our first approach was to train the VAE on historical data and reserve the final two years of our dataset as a temporal test set. However, the model exhibited significantly higher reconstruction error on these held-out final years compared to the training set. To address this, we transitioned from a temporal split to a spatial holdout strategy, training the model across all years while holding out a random 20% sample of counties. Rather than forcing the model to forecast future states, this approach reframed the objective toward spatial interpolation across unobserved counties—a theoretical shift that improved reconstruction performance.

The failure of the temporal split highlights the fact that data center deployment accelerates rapidly near the end of our timeline (@fig-estabs-over-time), and average facility scale increases over time. Consequently, the economic relationships in the final two years differed structurally from preceding periods, making temporal extrapolation less reliable than spatial interpolation.

Directly traversing the continuous latent space along a "data center vector" proved operationally difficult. To overcome this, we adopted a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) architecture using categorical conditioning embeddings. We grouped the log-transformed data center counts into six discrete bins (ranging from 0 to 6). These were passed into an embedding layer—a 6×4 weight matrix—allowing the network to learn discrete, non-linear economic impacts across different operational scales. This embedding was injected into both the encoder input and the latent space prior to decoding. To account for longitudinal shifts across our 16-year timeline, we applied a parallel 16×8 year embedding matrix to capture macro-level time trends.

Treatment effects were measured by comparing the baseline reconstruction (passing true county data through the full network) against a counterfactual pass where the data center conditioning bin was shifted upward before passing through the decoder. Subtracting baseline output from the counterfactual output yielded the predicted treatment effect across all economic features.

A critical limitation of our current CVAE is that shifting the data center condition upward causes the decoder to predict positive increases across every economic variable. This contradicts our Difference-in-Differences findings, which indicate that while certain economic indicators improve with data center presence, others decline. In future work, we plan to remove the explicit year embedding. Conditioning directly on year causes the model to overfit to single-year macroeconomic snapshots rather than learning each county's underlying temporal trajectories. Removing the year condition will force the latent space to encode longitudinal evolution directly, producing more nuanced and realistic counterfactual predictions.
